academic_bew.name: Generic ballot (Bafumi, Erikson & Wlezien)
academic_bew.citation: Bafumi, Erikson & Wlezien, 'Balancing, Generic Polls and Midterm Congressional Elections', Journal of Politics 72(3), 2010
academic_bew.attribution: Our implementation of BEW's published midterm equations, run on our generic-ballot average.
notes: tide is BEW's vote equation; their separate seats equation is reported as a diagnostic and is not used downstream

academic_referendum.name: Referendum (approval + income, no exposure)
academic_referendum.citation: Tufte, 'Determinants of the Outcomes of Midterm Congressional Elections', APSR 69(3), 1975; the modern version is Lewis-Beck & Tien
academic_referendum.attribution: Our fit of the referendum specification. NOT Lewis-Beck & Tien's published forecast.

inputs.approval_source: mean of 8 adults-sample approval poll(s) in the 14 days to 2026-08-27. Gallup interviewed adults, and so does this average; the residual house effect between Gallup and the rest of the adults field is under two points and cannot be re-measured now that Gallup has stopped polling, so it is left in the error bar rather than corrected for (Silver Bulletin poll list, aggregate only)
inputs.income_source: FRED income_growth_ytd as of 2026-08-27, 7 month(s) of the year in hand

benchmark.claim: Republicans lose about 28 House seats and the House
benchmark.authors: Charles Tien and Michael S. Lewis-Beck
benchmark.note: their DV is seat change, ours is vote share — the comparison is directional, not a reproduction

notes: no exposure term — this is the unconditioned referendum specification, and the gap against our fundamentals model IS the finding

academic_economic_pessimism.name: Economic pessimism (Lockerbie)
academic_economic_pessimism.citation: Lockerbie, 'The Challenge of Forecasting the 2024 Presidential and House Elections: Economic Pessimism and Election Outcomes', PS: Political Science & Politics, 2024
academic_economic_pessimism.attribution: Our implementation of Lockerbie's published House equation. The open-seat term's SIGN is our assumption, not his — see the sensitivity table.

inputs.pct_expect_worse_source: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers, Table 8, WORSE OFF row, monthly, 2026-06 (carried forward from 2026-06)
inputs.year_direction_label: a bad year for the president's party — the midterm rule
inputs.open_seats_source: 60 House incumbents had announced they were not seeking re-election by 2026-08-27 — Ballotpedia's dated list, entered by hand, read 2026-08-25

diagnostics.midterm_rule: Lockerbie: 'Midterms are, by definition, a bad year for the incumbent party.' The -1 is his rule, not our assumption.

sensitivity_year_direction.label: a bad year for the president's party — the midterm rule
a good year for the president's party

notes: forecasts SEAT CHANGE directly — the margin shown is our own seat curve run backwards from that seat count, and is not a number Lockerbie publishes

OUTSIDE THE FITTED RANGE on pct_expect_worse = 37, above the sample maximum of 32 and open_seats = 60, above the sample maximum of 56. The model was fit on 1952-2022 and this is a linear extrapolation beyond anything in that sample, which is most of why it is the most Democratic forecast on this site.
Lockerbie: 'Midterms are, by definition, a bad year for the incumbent party.' The -1 is his rule, not our assumption.
published out-of-sample mean absolute error is 16.8 seats — the interval is his, not ours, and it is very wide

academic_political_history.name: Political history (Lewis-Beck & Quinlan)
academic_political_history.citation: Lewis-Beck & Quinlan, 'A Political History Forecast of the 2024 US Congressional Elections', PS: Political Science & Politics 58(2), 2025, Table 1
academic_political_history.attribution: Our implementation of their published Table 1 equations. Forecasts both chambers directly.

inputs.structural_source: 4 Democratic Senate retirement(s) known by 2026-08-27 — UNAUDITED automatic draft from Wikipedia revision history — not yet checked by a person; governors: 24 — steps at the November 2025 elections, when Virginia flipped R to D and New Jersey held

benchmark.claim: Democrats lose Senate control with a net loss of three seats; House a knife-edge race at 215 D seats
benchmark.note: their 2024 forecast, quoted so our implementation can be sanity-checked against the published one

notes: forecasts SEAT COUNTS directly from institutional facts — no polls, no economy, no popularity. The margin shown is our seat curve run backwards from its House number, not theirs

academic_state_approval_economy.name: State approval + state economy (Enns et al.)
academic_state_approval_economy.citation: Enns, Lagodny, Colner & Kumar, 'Understanding Biden's Exit and the 2024 Election: The State Presidential Approval-State Economy Model', PS: Political Science & Politics, October 2024
academic_state_approval_economy.attribution: Not implemented. Listed so the gap is visible.
missing: state-level presidential approval estimates (MRP from national poll microdata)
state-level economic series (FRED has state personal income and unemployment; we capture neither, and the paper's choice of series is unread)
